newsitem.title: USA: Rubin says G7 will discuss emerging economies.
newsitem.headline: Rubin says G7 will discuss emerging economies.

text.p: The Group of Seven wealthy industrial countries is expected to explore measures to strengthen emerging market financial systems and fight entrenched corruption when they meet Sunday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Friday.
"Promoting reform ... to transform more developing countries into dynamic emerging markets is clearly in the interest of the United States," Rubin told reporters.

Finance ministers and central bank chiefs from the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- will gather Sunday on the fringes of the semiannual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
"We are moving toward consensus on a strategy to strengthen emerging market financial systems," Rubin said. "This is critically important to reduce the risks of future financial crises."

The United States is also pushing for a broad international initiative to fight corruption worldwide, Rubin said, adding, "We also urge the IMF and the multilateral development banks to expand the scope of their activities in the anticorruption area."
The G7 will discuss currency movements and the state of the global economy. They will also review steps to help Africa.

World Bank President James Wolfensohn told reporters the development institution has been working with emerging market countries so they are better prepared for the economic shock of foreign investors suddenly taking their money elsewhere.

"What we are trying to do is to make sure that the financial strength of the local markets are such that they can withstand at least to a stronger degree the shocks of international flows of money," he said.
His remarks came amid expectations that increases in U.S. interest rates and a retreat of stocks on Wall Street could lead to a leveling off of foreign investment in emerging economies.

The World Bank president also strongly defended the debt relief initiative for heavily indebted poor countries, saying he was proud of what had been accomplished and dismayed by criticism that it hadn't gone faster or included larger amounts of debt relief.
"I was hoping in my dreams that when all this happened I would get a standing ovation," a clearly frustrated Wolfensohn told reporters. "Instead of which people say, 'You're a son of a bitch.'"
The IMF and World Bank earlier this week approved a debt relief plan for Uganda, the first recipient of the debt relief intiative, promising the country $338 million in April 1998.
Critics have charged that the country has worked hard for many years to reform its economy and should have gotten the money quicker rather than having to wait another year.

But Wolfensohn said he believed the program was moving ahead quickly and said he expected the two lending agencies would approve relief for other good economic performers -- Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso and Bolivia -- this summer.
He also said countries could not enjoy the full fruits of economic revival and reform if they did not work to stamp out pervasive corruption.

He believed the issue of corruption and its impact on economic activity had been moved to the top of the agenda in many parts of the world and that while the World Bank could not serve as an international policeman, it was strongly encouraging governments to root it out.
